title: William Christian of Beargrass
summary: Virginia militia colonel William Christian moved to Jefferson County in 1785, directed defense of the Louisville settlements, and was killed in 1786.
bodyMarkdown:
William Christian spent most of his life on the Virginia frontier. He died in Kentucky's first years, defending the Louisville settlements. His life, told in [a biography of William Christian](https://grokipedia.com/page/William_Christian_(Virginia_politician)), connects the Revolution in western Virginia with the hard early years around the Falls of the Ohio.

## A Virginia frontier family

Christian was born about 1742 in Augusta County, Virginia. His parents, Israel Christian and Elizabeth Starke, were immigrants from Ireland who settled in Staunton in 1740 and ran a general store. As a young man he served as a captain in the Anglo-Cherokee War of 1758–1761. In the mid-1760s he read law under Patrick Henry and married Henry's sister Annie, although there is no evidence that he ever practiced law.

## Revolution and the Cherokee war

Christian represented Fincastle County in the House of Burgesses. In 1774 he led Fincastle militia in Dunmore's War but arrived too late for the Battle of Point Pleasant. He signed the Fincastle Resolutions, which Wikipedia calls the earliest statement of armed resistance to the British Crown in the colonies. He also served on the county's Committee of Safety. In 1776 he became colonel of the 1st Virginia Regiment.

That year, Cherokee forces under Dragging Canoe and Oconostota, allied with Britain, went to war with Virginia. Christian resigned his Continental commission to lead an expedition against the Overhill Cherokee towns. There was little combat, but his men destroyed Cherokee towns, which compelled some chiefs to agree to peace. Christian was one of the commissioners for the Treaty of Long Island of the Holston, signed July 20, 1777, and for a second Cherokee treaty in 1781.

## To Beargrass Creek

In 1785 Christian moved his family and enslaved people to what became Jefferson County, Kentucky. He claimed 9,000 acres as a bounty for his military service and started a plantation near Alexander Scott Bullitt, who married one of his daughters. Wikipedia notes that although the Revolution had ended, "Native Americans continued to defend their lands against occupation by American settlers."

The Christians set up [Fort William](https://grokipedia.com/page/fort_william_(kentucky)), and from there Christian directed the defense of the Louisville settlements. The fort is described as another name for A'Sturgus Station, built in 1779 on the Middle Fork of Beargrass Creek. The same article says Annie Christian began calling the site Fort William only after her husband's death.

## Death north of the Ohio

In 1786, as one of Kentucky's most experienced officers, Christian led an expedition against Native Americans north of the Ohio River. He was killed in a skirmish on April 9, near present-day Jeffersonville, Indiana. His troops brought his body back for burial in the Bullitt family cemetery at Oxmoor. Annie moved east and died in 1790.

## Kentucky today

The Christians' early log house still stands. [Christian County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Christian_County,_Kentucky), formed in 1797 with Hopkinsville as its seat, carries his name. A historical marker for Fort William stands in front of the Eight Mile House near St. Matthews and Lyndon, although the fort itself was southwest of that house. For the wider defense of the Falls settlements, see [George Rogers Clark](/stories/george-rogers-clark/).
